claim: The province's towns and peoples can be fixed by coordinates taken from itineraries and reports.
evidence_note: The ancient testimony itself, standing at the head of the corpus and deriving from nothing else in it.
uncertainty: The coordinates are stretched by the travel times they were computed from, and the catalogue thins to hearsay north of the Carpathians.
notes: Recorded so that the ancient evidence states its claim like everything else, rather than sitting in the corpus as an unexamined baseline.

claim: The ancient province can be restored to the map from the ancient authors.
evidence_note: The Parergon sheet is drawn from the classical authors, Ptolemy among them, and says so in its own apparatus.
uncertainty: The restoration is a reading of texts, not a survey, and its coastline and river courses are inherited rather than observed.
notes: A derivation that can be evidenced, which is why it is allowed to be one.

claim: The province's sites and roads can be established by combining ancient testimony with excavation.
evidence_note: The series' method is to reconcile the ancient itineraries and catalogues with the archaeological record, and it cites both.
uncertainty: Site identifications in the series are themselves contested in places; the Roman baseline layer carries that as low confidence rather than flattening it.
notes: The reconstruction the shared GIS baseline follows, recorded here so the essay can say whose reconstruction it is.

claim: The frontiers of 1920 recover a territory that antiquity had already defined.
evidence_note: The class works by placing a modern frontier beside an ancient one and letting the resemblance argue.
uncertainty: No individual sheet has been selected from this class, so the claim is characterised at class level and no particular map is being described.
notes: Recorded as responding to the antiquarian tradition rather than deriving from it: the resemblance is the rhetorical move, not an inheritance anyone has evidenced.

claim: Present inhabitants descend, unbroken, from the Dacians the Romans found.
evidence_note: The class reaches past the Roman province to a pre-Roman one, using ancient testimony as a starting point rather than as support.
uncertainty: This is the claim the trench describes and does not adjudicate. Rubric rr-1 forbids using any map here to settle a question about who anyone is today.
notes: Recorded so the essay can show the claim being made. The corpus takes no position on the descent question itself, and nothing here may be read as taking one.

claim: A map that looks like a historical map carries a historical map's authority.
evidence_note: Resemblance only. No derivation is claimed or evidenced, and none may be inferred from the similarity itself.
uncertainty: Creator and source are unidentified, which is what makes the item reception rather than evidence however detailed it appears.
notes: The load-bearing row of this table, and the visual counterpart of the homonym_only edge in Nomen Errans: a shared appearance is not a relationship, and the corpus says so in a row rather than leaving a reader to join them by eye.
